title: Hidden Fisher Information in Many-Body Quantum Sensors

paper.title: Hidden Fisher Information in Many-Body Quantum Sensors
paper.abstract: Abstract Quantum Fisher information (QFI) determines the ultimate precision of a quantum sensor after optimization over all allowed measurements, but it does not quantify how difficult the optimal readout is to implement. We introduce a moment Fisher hierarchy F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} , which measures the fraction of QFI accessible to collective spin moments up to degree k k , together with a readout-complexity scale k 90 k_{90} defined by the minimum degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of the QFI. Applying this framework to a nonlinear collective-spin sensor, we show that many-body dynamics can preserve large QFI while transferring the optimal readout into high-rank S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) tensor sectors inaccessible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to N = 100 N=100 , first moments access only ∼ 10 − 2 \sim 10^{-2} of the available QFI, while the degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of it grows to k 90 ≃ 28 k_{90}\simeq 28 . A rank-resolved analysis of the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) under weak damping shows that the nonlinear protocol pushes the optimal readout toward the highest available tensor ranks while strongly depleting its low-rank weight. These results identify nonlinear tangent-space shear as the mechanism behind a finite-size readout-complexity bottleneck in many-body quantum metrology.

sections.heading: I Moment hierarchy and endpoint completeness
sections.text: This section gives the operator-space structure underlying the moment Fisher hierarchy used in the main text. The system is restricted to the permutation-symmetric spin- j = N / 2 j=N/2 irreducible representation, whose Hilbert-space dimension is d = N + 1 . d=N+1. (31) The collective spin matrices are represented in the J z J_{z} basis with magnetic quantum numbers m = − j , − j + 1 , … , j . m=-j,-j+1,\ldots,j. (32) The real moment space ℳ k {\cal M}_{k} consists of traceless Hermitian collective spin polynomials of degree at most k k . Equivalently, in the spin- j j irreducible representation, the collective operator algebra decomposes into irreducible S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) tensor ranks ℓ = 0 , 1 , … , 2 ​ j = N . \ell=0,1,\ldots,2j=N. (33) The rank- ℓ \ell sector has dimension 2 ​ ℓ + 1 2\ell+1 . Therefore, the full traceless operator space has dimension ∑ ℓ = 1 N ( 2 ​ ℓ + 1 ) = ( N + 1 ) 2 − 1 = N ⁡ ( N + 2 ) . \sum_{\ell=1}^{N}(2\ell+1)=(N+1)^{2}-1=N(N+2). (34) Collective spin polynomials of degree k k generate tensor ranks up to ℓ = k \ell=k . Therefore, collective spin polynomials of degree N N generate the full traceless operator algebra, ℳ N = { all ​ traceless ​ Hermitian ​ operators ​ on ​ the ​ spin ​ - ​ j ​ manifold } . {\cal M}_{N}=\{\mathrm{all\ traceless\ Hermitian\ operators\ on\ the\ spin}\text{-}j\ \mathrm{manifold}\}. (35) This establishes the finite- N N completeness of the hierarchy. The endpoint completeness is essential for interpreting the results. The SLD L α L_{\alpha} is Hermitian but need not be Hilbert–Schmidt traceless. This does not affect the hierarchy, because adding a multiple of the identity to an estimator changes neither its variance nor its parameter response, since Tr ⁡ ( ∂ α ρ α ) = 0 \mathrm{Tr}(\partial_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha})=0 . We may therefore use the traceless representative L ~ α = L α − Tr ⁡ ( L α ) d ​ 𝕀 , \widetilde{L}_{\alpha}=L_{\alpha}-\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(L_{\alpha})}{d}\,\mathbb{I}, (36) which belongs to ℳ N {\cal M}_{N} . Measuring L α L_{\alpha} locally saturates the QFI, and the identity shift is operationally irrelevant; hence the complete hierarchy satisfies F M ( N ) = F Q , η N = F M ( N ) F Q = 1 . F_{M}^{(N)}=F_{Q},\qquad\eta_{N}=\frac{F_{M}^{(N)}}{F_{Q}}=1. (37) In the numerical calculations, this endpoint recovery is explicitly verified for every hierarchy curve used in the figures. This check distinguishes hidden Fisher information from numerical loss of QFI. If η N ≃ 1 \eta_{N}\simeq 1 but η k ≪ 1 \eta_{k}\ll 1 for small k k , the information is present in the state but inaccessible to low-degree moment estimators.

F_{X}=\frac{(\partial_{\alpha}\langle X\rangle)^{2}}{(\Delta X)^{2}}=\frac{(c^{T}g)^{2}}{c^{T}\Sigma c}. (41) Maximizing over the real coefficient vector c c gives F M ( k ) = g k T ​ Σ k + ​ g k , η k = F M ( k ) F Q , F_{M}^{(k)}=g_{k}^{T}\Sigma_{k}^{+}g_{k},\qquad\eta_{k}=\frac{F_{M}^{(k)}}{F_{Q}}, (42) where Σ k + \Sigma_{k}^{+} is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. If the covariance matrix is nonsingular, Eq. ( 42 ) reduces to g k T ​ Σ k − 1 ​ g k g_{k}^{T}\Sigma_{k}^{-1}g_{k} . If null directions are present, the pseudoinverse gives the correct variational result provided covariance-null directions are handled consistently. In the mixed-state calculations, the covariance matrix is diagonalized and only positive eigenvalue directions are retained. This avoids artificial enhancement from numerically singular directions. The readout-complexity scale used throughout the paper is k 90 = min ⁡ { k : η k ≥ 0.9 } . k_{90}=\min\{k:\eta_{k}\geq 0.9\}. (43) Small k 90 k_{90} means that the QFI is directly visible to low-order collective moments. A large and system-size-dependent k 90 k_{90} means that the QFI is present but distributed over increasingly high-degree collective correlations. The hierarchy should be interpreted as an accessibility hierarchy for moment estimators, not as a restricted-POVM optimization. A full number-resolved histogram, a parity measurement, a randomized measurement protocol, or an interaction-based decoder may access information beyond F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} at fixed low k k . This distinction is important because the hierarchy is designed to diagnose when such additional readout resources become necessary.

sections.heading: III Efficient pure-state hierarchy for large N N
sections.text: The large- N N calculations in the main text use unitary kicked-top dynamics and exploit a pure-state version of the hierarchy. sections.heading: VIII Relation to classical Fisher information of explicit collective measurements
sections.text: The moment hierarchy is not a restricted-POVM optimization. It optimizes the best scalar error-propagation estimator formed from collective moments up to degree k k . By contrast, for a specified POVM { Π x } \{\Pi_{x}\} , the classical Fisher information is F C ​ [ { Π x } ] = ∑ x [ ∂ α Tr ⁡ ( ρ α ​ Π x ) ] 2 Tr ⁡ ( ρ α ​ Π x ) . F_{C}[\{\Pi_{x}\}]=\sum_{x}\frac{[\partial_{\alpha}\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\alpha}\Pi_{x})]^{2}}{\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\alpha}\Pi_{x})}. (55) The QFI is the supremum of F C F_{C} over all POVMs. Therefore, F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} should be interpreted as the Fisher information accessible to a specified low-degree moment estimator, not as the best possible Fisher information under every measurement compatible with collective hardware. To make this distinction explicit, we compute the classical Fisher information for two concrete collective readouts. First, we consider a global rotation followed by number-resolved measurement in the J z J_{z} basis. Such readouts implicitly contain high-order statistics of the collective distribution and therefore exceed the low-degree scalar moment hierarchy at fixed k k . This comparison clarifies the operational meaning of hidden Fisher information. The suppression of η 1 \eta_{1} diagnoses a limitation of low-order moment readout, not an absence of QFI and not a fundamental failure of all collective measurements. A full histogram, a parity measurement, or an active decoder supplies additional readout resources. The moment hierarchy quantifies when such resources become necessary. sections.heading: XI Experimental observables and reconstruction
sections.text: Degree one consists of the collective spin components J x J_{x} , J y J_{y} , and J z J_{z} . Degree two includes second moments, spin-squeezing observables, and spin-noise covariances. Higher degrees correspond to higher-order cumulants or symmetrized collective-spin products. Depending on the platform, these quantities can be accessed through repeated collective measurements after global rotations, spin-noise spectroscopy, randomized measurements, parity-sensitive detection, number-resolved histograms, or interaction-based decoding. The hierarchy separates limitations of state preparation from limitations of readout. If an independent calculation or certification indicates large QFI while F M ( 1 ) F_{M}^{(1)} and F M ( 2 ) F_{M}^{(2)} remain much smaller, then the missing sensitivity lies outside the low-degree moment sector. A direct experimental test is therefore to compare the same probe before and after a richer readout operation. Recovery of Fisher information after an echo, time-reversal sequence, interaction-based decoder, parity-sensitive measurement, or number-resolved measurement would demonstrate conversion of high-complexity metrological information into a readable signal. The hierarchy does not rank these readout strategies by hardware cost. Its role is to provide a common operational benchmark: a readout architecture is successful when it closes the gap between the Fisher information available in the state and that accessible to the initially restricted low-degree observables.

Box 19395-5531, Tehran, Iran October 24, 2026 Abstract Quantum Fisher information (QFI) determines the ultimate precision of a quantum sensor after optimization over all allowed measurements, but it does not quantify how difficult the optimal readout is to implement. We introduce a moment Fisher hierarchy F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} , which measures the fraction of QFI accessible to collective spin moments up to degree k k , together with a readout-complexity scale k 90 k_{90} defined by the minimum degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of the QFI. Applying this framework to a nonlinear collective-spin sensor, we show that many-body dynamics can preserve large QFI while transferring the optimal readout into high-rank S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) tensor sectors inaccessible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to N = 100 N=100 , first moments access only ∼ 10 − 2 \sim 10^{-2} of the available QFI, while the degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of it grows to k 90 ≃ 28 k_{90}\simeq 28 . A rank-resolved analysis of the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) under weak damping shows that the nonlinear protocol pushes the optimal readout toward the highest available tensor ranks while strongly depleting its low-rank weight. These results identify nonlinear tangent-space shear as the mechanism behind a finite-size readout-complexity bottleneck in many-body quantum metrology. Introduction.— Quantum-enhanced metrology aims to measure weak signals with a precision that cannot be reached by independent particles alone [ 26 , 28 ] . The central idea is to use nonclassical many-body states—for example, spin-squeezed [ 61 , 40 , 44 ] , strongly entangled [ 59 , 54 , 7 ] , critical [ 62 ] , or dynamically correlated states [ 22 , 21 ] —as probes whose response to an unknown parameter is amplified by quantum correlations. In this setting, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) has become the standard theoretical benchmark [ 52 , 15 ] . Given a parameter α \alpha encoded in a probe state ρ α \rho_{\alpha} , the QFI F Q F_{Q} determines the best possible local sensitivity through the quantum Cramér–Rao bound [ 34 , 35 , 8 ] . It tells us how much metrological information is contained in the quantum state when the measurement is allowed to be fully optimized [ 27 ] . Although the QFI gives the ultimate achievable precision, it does not quantify the complexity of the measurement required to attain that precision [ 17 , 48 ] . In many-body systems, the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) defining the optimal readout can become a highly nonlocal operator [ 64 ] . It often retains little overlap with experimentally accessible observables such as collective magnetization or low-order correlations [ 55 , 23 ] . A many-body sensor may therefore possess large QFI while remaining operationally difficult to read out. This readout issue has become increasingly relevant because experimental platforms have made remarkable progress in preparing correlated many-body probes. Metrologically useful correlations have been generated across multiple highly controlled physical systems. For example, in cavity-QED ensembles, light-matter interactions create robust entangled states [ 41 , 36 , 2 ] , with recent advances demonstrating complex programmable interactions [ 53 , 31 , 51 ] . Similar metrological potential has been unlocked in trapped ions [ 5 , 46 , 38 ] and spinor condensates [ 42 , 63 ] . Concurrently, Rydberg arrays and optical clocks have shown that strong dipole interactions can generate states with immense metrological capability [ 6 , 25 , 10 , 4 , 56 ] . These systems show that many-body interactions can create states with strong metrological potential. At the same time, they also show that state preparation alone is not sufficient: the experimentally observed sensitivity often depends crucially on the final readout. This realization has motivated several advanced measurement strategies. Interaction-based readout and phase magnification transform complicated correlations into simpler, readable signals [ 58 , 14 , 37 , 50 ] . Time reversal effectively disentangles the probe prior to detection [ 45 , 13 ] . Meanwhile, parity-sensitive detection and number-resolved measurements extract fine-grained quantum features [ 24 , 39 ] . Furthermore, randomized measurement protocols and variational approaches reconstruct state properties without demanding full tomography [ 11 , 19 , 9 , 30 , 33 , 3 ] . These methods can be understood as ways of decoding, amplifying, or reconstructing many-body information before it is finally measured. Their success points to a basic question: when is such an advanced readout merely helpful, and when is it necessary? This question is not only technical, but also interpretational. In many experiments, the same observed sensitivity can be limited either by imperfect state preparation or by an insufficiently expressive measurement. Without a diagnostic that separates these two possibilities, a state with large hidden metrological response may be mistaken for a state with little metrological value. A central aim of the present work is to make this distinction operational. At present, this question lacks a compact degree-resolved diagnostic. The QFI gives the best possible sensitivity over all measurements. The classical Fisher information gives the sensitivity of one specified measurement. Between these two extremes, we need a tool that quantifies how much of the QFI is accessible when the experiment is restricted to a controlled family of simple observables. For collective spin sensors, a natural family is given by collective moments. First moments describe ordinary collective magnetization. Second moments include spin-squeezing and covariance measurements [ 23 ] . Higher moments probe increasingly complex many-body correlations. A hierarchy organized by moment degree therefore provides a direct measure of readout complexity. Existing approaches typically characterize either the ultimate metrological sensitivity through the QFI or the performance of a particular measurement protocol. By contrast, the present hierarchy resolves how metrological information is distributed across collective operator complexity. This identifies a distinct notion of hidden Fisher information: information that remains present in the quantum state but is inaccessible to low-degree collective readout. The hierarchy therefore provides a quantitative bridge between metrological sensitivity and experimentally accessible measurement complexity. Here we introduce such a hierarchy. For each integer k k , we define the moment Fisher information F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} as the maximum error-propagation Fisher information obtainable from scalar estimators built from collective spin polynomials of degree at most k k . The normalized quantity η k = F M ( k ) F Q \eta_{k}=\frac{F_{M}^{(k)}}{F_{Q}} (1) measures the fraction of the QFI accessible to collective moments up to degree k k . We also define the readout-complexity scale k 90 = min ⁡ { k : F M ( k ) ≥ 0.9 ​ F Q } , k_{90}=\min\{k:\,F_{M}^{(k)}\geq 0.9F_{Q}\}, (2) which is the minimum collective moment degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of the QFI. A small k 90 k_{90} means that the metrological information is directly visible to low-order collective readout. A large, system-size-dependent k 90 k_{90} means that the state contains useful information, but that the information is distributed over high-order collective correlations. The moment Fisher hierarchy complements, rather than replaces, the QFI. The QFI asks what is possible if the measurement is unrestricted. The hierarchy asks what remains accessible when the readout is restricted to collective moments of bounded degree. This distinction is important because many experiments do not directly implement arbitrary many-body measurements. They typically access low-order collective observables, possibly after global rotations, unless additional resources such as time reversal, interaction-based decoding, number resolution, randomized measurements, or tomography are supplied. Thus, F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} provides a practical way to diagnose whether a sensor is limited by state preparation or by readout complexity. To demonstrate the hierarchy in a controlled many-body setting, we study a kicked collective spin, corresponding to a symmetric-subspace realization of the quantum kicked top [ 32 , 12 ] . The kicked top provides a minimal nonlinear many-body sensor [ 49 , 60 , 57 ] in which the full collective operator hierarchy can be resolved at finite N N . It provides a tunable non-Gaussian framework where the QFI can be compared directly with accessible moment Fisher information, and the structure of the optimal readout can be resolved in operator space. We find a sharp separation between information storage and information accessibility. In the linear protocol, the QFI is almost completely accessible through first moments. In the resonant nonlinear protocol, by contrast, the QFI remains present but becomes largely invisible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to N = 100 N=100 , first moments access only about 10 − 2 10^{-2} of the QFI, while the degree required to recover 90 % 90\% of the information grows to k 90 ≃ 28 k_{90}\simeq 28 . The endpoint of the hierarchy recovers the QFI, confirming that the information is not lost. Instead, it is redistributed into high-degree collective moment sectors. We identify the physical mechanism as nonlinear tangent-space shear. The parameter derivative of the state initially corresponds to a smooth displacement on the collective Bloch sphere. Strong nonlinear kicking stretches this tangent direction into fine angular structures. In operator language, the associated optimal readout, represented locally by the SLD, acquires substantial weight in high-rank irreducible S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) tensor sectors [ 18 , 47 ] . Since collective moments of degree k k resolve tensor ranks only up to ℓ = k \ell=k , this redistribution makes the optimal readout progressively inaccessible to low-degree moments. This gives a direct geometric interpretation of hidden Fisher information: the state is sensitive to the parameter, but the observable that reveals this sensitivity has become a high-rank many-body operator. Because the mechanism relies on nonlinear generation of high-rank collective operator structure, it is expected to arise broadly in non-Gaussian many-body sensors beyond the kicked-top setting. Our contribution is therefore threefold. First, we introduce a finite- N N moment Fisher hierarchy that quantifies how much QFI is accessible to collective moment readout of a given degree. Second, we define k 90 k_{90} as an operational readout-complexity scale for many-body sensors. Third, we show that nonlinear many-body dynamics can preserve QFI while moving the optimal readout into high-rank operator sectors, thereby making the information hidden from standard low-order measurements. Relation to richer collective measurements.— The moment hierarchy deliberately focuses on low-degree scalar moment estimators. It therefore does not exclude the possibility that other collective measurements recover more information. Indeed, the Supplemental Material compares the hierarchy with explicit collective readouts based on optimized global rotations followed by number-resolved J z J_{z} histograms or parity measurements. These readouts can recover substantially more information than linear moments because a full histogram contains high-order statistics of the collective distribution. This is not a contradiction. It confirms the interpretation of F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} as a resource diagnostic: when low-degree moments fail, one must supply additional readout resources, such as number resolution, parity sensitivity, tomography, randomized measurements, or interaction-based decoding. Experimental readout bottlenecks and future tests.— The present results clarify a limitation that is common to many existing many-body metrology experiments. Most platforms have become highly successful at preparing correlated probes, but the final measurement is often still organized around a small set of low-order collective observables: mean spin, spin noise, covariance matrices, number imbalance, or a few rotated collective components [ 41 , 36 , 2 , 5 , 42 , 63 , 6 , 25 ] . Such measurements are natural and powerful when the parameter response remains a smooth displacement or a Gaussian deformation of the collective state. They are not, however, guaranteed to reveal the information carried by a strongly non-Gaussian many-body probe. Our hierarchy gives a precise formulation of this limitation: a sensor may contain large QFI while the low-degree moment sector has small overlap with the SLD. In that regime, an experiment can fail to observe the predicted gain not because the useful quantum state was not created, but because the readout projects onto the wrong part of operator space. This distinction is especially important for nonlinear protocols, interaction-generated non-Gaussian states, Rydberg and optical-clock arrays, cavity-mediated ensembles, trapped ions, and spinor condensates, where the dynamics can generate fine angular structures on the collective Bloch sphere [ 53 , 31 , 51 , 46 , 38 , 10 , 4 , 56 ] . Conventional spin-squeezing or covariance measurements test only the first few layers of this structure. A null or weak signal in these observables should therefore not be interpreted automatically as absence of metrological information. It may instead indicate that the Fisher information has become hidden in high-rank collective correlations. In this sense, the relevant experimental question is not only whether a many-body state has been prepared, but whether the apparatus has enough readout resolution to match the operator complexity of the optimal measurement. The hierarchy suggests a direct experimental protocol. One first estimates or bounds the QFI using existing certification, randomized measurement, or variational methods [ 11 , 19 , 9 , 30 , 33 , 3 ] . One then reconstructs the accessible Fisher information from progressively higher collective moments, or from controlled families of rotated collective measurements. If F M ( 1 ) F_{M}^{(1)} or F M ( 2 ) F_{M}^{(2)} nearly saturates F Q F_{Q} , the sensor is readout-simple and standard collective detection is sufficient. If instead F M ( k ) ≪ F Q F_{M}^{(k)}\ll F_{Q} until k k becomes large, the experiment is readout-limited: the missing metrological gain is stored in correlations that ordinary collective readout cannot resolve. The scale k 90 k_{90} therefore acts as an experimentally meaningful “readout depth”, analogous to a resolution requirement for the measurement rather than a property of state preparation alone. This viewpoint also reinterprets advanced readout methods. Interaction-based readout, phase magnification, and time reversal [ 58 , 14 , 37 , 50 , 45 , 13 ] should be understood as physical decoders that rotate a high-rank SLD back toward a low-degree observable before detection. Parity-sensitive and number-resolved measurements [ 24 , 39 ] provide a different route: rather than simplifying the SLD, they measure finer features of the collective distribution and thereby access higher-order information directly. In the language of the present work, a successful decoder or high-resolution measurement closes the gap between F Q F_{Q} and F M ( 1 ) F_{M}^{(1)} or F M ( 2 ) F_{M}^{(2)} . Thus, future experiments can test hidden Fisher information by measuring the same state before and after an echo, time-reversal, or interaction-based decoding sequence: closing the hierarchy gap would directly demonstrate the conversion of high-rank metrological information into a readable low-degree signal. Conclusion.— We have shown that many-body quantum sensors can possess large QFI while rendering most of it inaccessible to standard low-order collective moment readout. This separation is not captured by the QFI alone, because the QFI optimizes over all possible measurements and therefore hides the cost of implementing the optimal readout. To quantify this cost, we introduced a moment Fisher hierarchy F M ( k ) F_{M}^{(k)} and the associated readout-complexity scale k 90 k_{90} . In the driven collective spin studied here, first moments access only a percent-level fraction of the QFI by N = 100 N=100 , while recovering 90 % 90\% of it requires a moment degree k 90 ≃ 28 k_{90}\simeq 28 . The rank-resolved SLD calculation independently shows that nonlinear dynamics transfers the locally optimal readout toward the highest available S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) tensor ranks and suppresses its low-rank weight to the 10 − 3 10^{-3} scale under weak damping. Our results show that metrological usefulness is determined not only by how much QFI a many-body state contains, but also by whether the available measurement resolves the operator sector in which that information resides. Hidden Fisher information therefore turns the usual question of quantum metrology into a joint state-readout problem: a many-body probe may be highly sensitive, yet experimentally silent, until an appropriate decoder or high-order measurement is supplied. The moment Fisher hierarchy provides a quantitative diagnostic of this accessibility and identifies readout complexity as a genuine bottleneck in many-body quantum sensing.
